results.title: AWS Raised GPU Prices Twice in Six Months: What It Signals and What to Do About It - Data Storage
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
An AWS p5e.48xlarge Capacity Block reservation, eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs bundled into a single instance, cost $34.61 an hour in December 2025. AWS raised that rate to $39.80 on January 4, 2026, a quiet, weekend announcement with no advance customer notice. Then, on July 1, 2026, AWS raised it again, this time to roughly $47.76 an hour. That's a 38 percent cumulative increase in six months, on a product enterprises specifically pay a premium for because it guarantees GPU capacity will be there when a training run needs to start.

...

## The Two Hikes, Side by Side

| Metric | January 4, 2026 | July 1, 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increase | ~15% | ~20% |
| Families affected | P5e, P5en (H200-based) | P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, P4de |
| Example: p5e.48xlarge | $34.61 to $39.80/hr | $39.80 to ~$47.76/hr |
| Advance notice | None, posted over a weekend | Published on AWS documentation page |

The January hike affected P5e and P5en instances specifically, the H200-based families. The July hike was broader, covering P6-B300 and P6-B200 (AWS's Blackwell-generation instances), plus P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, essentially AWS's entire GPU reservation lineup. Older instance families saw smaller dollar increases but similar percentage jumps, meaning this wasn't a single product line getting repriced, it was the whole Capacity Blocks catalog.

The new July 1 rate card, per accelerator-hour in US regions:

| Instance Family | New Rate (per accelerator-hour) |
| --- | --- |
| P6-B300 (Blackwell) | $14.04 |
| P6-B200 (Blackwell) | $12.355 |
| P5en (US) | $6.865 |
| P5e (US) | $5.97 |
| P5 (US) | $5.191 |
| P4de (US) | $2.214 |

...

Capacity Blocks for ML are AWS's reserve-ahead product: you commit to a fixed block of GPU accelerators for a defined future time window and pay upfront for the guarantee that hardware will be available when your window starts. This is what got the two hikes covered here.

Standard on-demand and Savings Plan pricing actually moved in the opposite direction over the past year. In June 2025, AWS cut on-demand pricing for P5 instances by up to 45 percent, P5en by up to 26 percent, and P4d and P4de by up to 33 percent. That cut is still in effect for those product types.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: Up 20% in 2026
results.author: Sofia Lindström
highlights:
AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

## Four rises in 2026, and where July’s 20% falls

According to eCorpIT, AWS made the July change on its pricing page without a blog post or customer advisory: the notice and the new rates appeared on the Capacity Blocks pricing page, and the October rise took the same route. AWS’s pricing page is therefore where a change shows up. The four steps eCorpIT lists, plus the date AWS has given for the next update:

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

The steps compound, so the total is larger than any single headline. TECHi puts January plus July at roughly 38% since December. VentureBeat counts four AWS Capacity Block increases in 2026. October lifts the total further, as the single-instance series below shows.

## Family by family: the October 7 rates

The table lists the October 7 rate per accelerator-hour for each family, as eCorpIT reports the schedule. eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, says AWS now lists one Capacity Block rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6, and puts P5 at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in all listed regions. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page also lists P4d, which is not among the six July families, at $1.696 per accelerator-hour for standard AWS regions, the cheapest Nvidia family on that schedule.

| Family | October 7 rate per accelerator-hour | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | $16.146 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $14.04 in July |
| P6-B200 | $14.208 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $12.355 in July |
| P5 | $5.970 | All listed regions, per eCorpIT; up 15% from $5.191 in US regions and about 26.5% from $4.72 outside the US, July rates |
| P5e | $6.866 | Up 15% from $5.97 in July; used in the p5e.48xlarge series below |
| P5en | $7.895 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $6.865 in US regions and about 26.5% from $6.241 elsewhere, July rates |
| P4de | $2.546 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $2.214 in US regions in July |
| P4d | $1.696 | Standard AWS regions, from AWS’s Capacity Blocks pricing page |

eCorpIT puts the October rise at 15% on most families, and P6-B300 shows it: $14.04 to $16.146 is 15%. P5 and P5en outside the US are the exception, at about 26.5%. That larger figure sits next to a change in how rates are listed, since eCorpIT’s page says AWS now lists one rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6.

...

A Capacity Block runs for 1 to 14 days or a multiple of 7 days up to 182 days, with up to 64 instances per block (512 GPUs at eight per instance), and it can be scheduled up to 8 weeks ahead, according to AWS’s Capacity Blocks documentation. AWS’s billing documentation says the block price is charged up front, with the payment landing on your account between 5 minutes and 12 hours after purchase. From the start of the block, the running charge is the operating system fee alone.

...

AWS’s stated reason, as eCorpIT quotes it, is that Capacity Block pricing varies with supply and demand and that the adjustment “reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.” ... Cloud economist Corey Quinn calls the change “a policy decision, not supply/demand”, on the grounds that AWS updated published base rates. Analyst Pareekh Jain says the “most defensible explanation is simply market-based pricing tied to supply and demand.”

The cadence leans toward Quinn’s reading, though it does not settle the question. Four rises in 2026 landed on January 3, April 1, July and October 7, each upward, and AWS has already named January 2027 for the next update. A list-price schedule reviewed each quarter can be announced ahead of time, and AWS’s own phrase “this quarter” fits that reading. Demand is still real, since Jain’s explanation and a schedule can both be true at once, and nothing in the sources rules out another step. January looks like a scheduled review that has gone up every time so far.

...

## A block is 13% under H100 on-demand list, and the neoclouds moved too

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

| GPU | Provider and product | Per GPU-hour | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | AWS Capacity Block (P5) | $5.970 | Rate from October 7 |
| H100 | AWS on-demand (p5.48xlarge, us-east-1) | $6.88 | Rank.ai, November 10 |
| H100 | Nebius on-demand | $4.50 | Raised October 1 |
| H200 | AWS Capacity Block (P5e) | $6.866 | Rate from October 7 |
| H200 | Nebius on-demand | $5.40 | Raised October 1 |
| B200 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B200) | $14.208 | Rate from October 7 |
| B200 | Nebius on-demand | $8.50 | Raised October 1 |
| B300 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B300) | $16.146 | Rate from October 7 |
| B300 | Nebius on-demand | $9.50 | Raised October 1 |

The Nebius figures come from Sesame Disk, which reports that Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates 17-21% on October 1, 2026; Nebius’s pricing page lists H100 at $4.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU hour. The same Sesame Disk report says CoreWeave added a 10% increase after a 25% rise in July, putting its pricing up roughly 37.5% since July. The neoclouds have been raising rates too. For Azure and Google Cloud H100 pricing, see our AWS, Azure and Google Cloud GPU pricing comparison, and for the H200 class on AMD’s side our AMD MI350P and Nvidia H200 comparison.

## Booking before January: an H100 block beats on-demand list only above 87% utilisation

Convergedigest reports that customers pay the prevailing rate when the reservation is purchased, even if the reserved capacity starts after a future price change. AWS’s billing documentation agrees on the mechanics: a search across a range of dates returns the lowest-priced offering available, and once you have reserved a block its price does not change. With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027” for that update, and the first 2026 rise landed on January 3, so do not assume you have the whole month. VentureBeat’s advice is to check Capacity Block rates before buying, since AWS has raised them four times in 2026.

Locking a rate is worth it only if you fill the block, because the whole block is charged up front. A block costs the same whether the GPUs are busy or idle, while on-demand bills only the hours used. The break-even utilisation is the block’s hourly price divided by the on-demand hourly price. For H100, $47.76 divided by $55.04 is 87%, so a block beats on-demand list only if you use at least 87% of its hours. A block also reserves the capacity, so 87% is the cost line and not the whole decision. The comparison sets the block’s reservation price against the on-demand rate and leaves out the separate OS fee.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing in 2026: Why AI Compute Costs Keep Rising | Aethir
highlights:
On July 1, 2026, Amazon Web Services raised rates for EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reservation service for AI accelerators, by roughly 20%, only six months after a 15% rise in January. Teams that reserve cloud GPU capacity have watched GPU cloud pricing climb by more than a third since the year began, and AI compute costs are rising across every roadmap that depends on reserved capacity.

Blackwell B300 instances moved to $14.04 per accelerator hour, while H100-based P5 capacity climbed to $5.191 dollars per hour in US regions. These are the most sought-after accelerators in the cloud GPU market.

AWS lifted the same rates by about 15% in January. Repeated increases on flagship instances signal a structural shift in GPU cloud pricing, not a ... Hyperscalers built their business on steadily falling prices as hardware improved. That era has ended because supply is constrained and demand keeps compounding.

results.title: Two AWS GPU Price Hikes in Six Months: Rethinking Your AI Compute Mix - Upendra Sengar Blog
results.author: Upendra Sengar
highlights:
In early July, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices 20% across its main GPU instance families. That is the second hike in six months, following a 15% increase on January 4. If you are on H100-based P5 instances, you are now paying $5.19 per GPU hour. B300 slots hit $14.04 per GPU hour. For a team running a p5e.48xlarge continuously, the January hike alone pushed the bill from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour. The July hike adds another layer on top of that.

...

The mistake I see teams make is treating these two markets as one question: "should we use cloud GPUs or APIs?" That framing is too coarse. The real question is what kind of compute you are actually buying, and which market it belongs to. AWS announced the July 1 increase in late June, affecting P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families. If your team missed that, check your bill.

results.title: GPU cost optimization is not rightsizing | PointFive Blog
results.author: Kevin Rhine
highlights: Pricing is also a problem again. AWS cut on-demand and Savings Plan prices on P4 and P5 instances by up to 45 percent in mid-2025. Reserved capacity moved the other way. Capacity Block pricing increased in several separate updates. P5e and P5en rates rose roughly 15 percent in January 2026. An April update raised commercial-region P6-B200 and US-region P5en rates by about 10 percent. On July 1, many commercial-region rates rose roughly 20 percent across P4de, P5, P5e, P5en, P6-B200 and P6-B300, with regional exceptions. An AWS spokesperson told The Register the January move "reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter." AWS said so itself in the very announcement that cut those prices: "The growth in demand for GPU capacity has outpaced industry-wide supply, making GPUs a scarce resource and increasing the cost of securing them."

results.title: AWS cuts prices of some EC2 Nvidia GPU-accelerated instances: What changed
results.author: iTechGuides Team
highlights:
AWS reduced On-Demand prices for P4d, P4de, P5, and P5en EC2 instances by up to 45%, but the reduction is not universal.

...

AWS cuts prices of some EC2 Nvidia GPU-accelerated instances by up to 45%, but the June 2025 change covers only the P5, P5en, P4d, and P4de families. Lower On-Demand rates began June 1, 2025, while updated Savings Plan pricing applied to purchases after June 4. Maximum reductions apply to Amazon Linux and vary by configuration.

## Key takeaways

- AWS announced maximum On-Demand reductions of 45% for P5, 26% for P5en, and 33% for both P4d and P4de instances.
- The reduced On-Demand prices took effect June 1, 2025; Savings Plan purchases received the updated pricing after June 4, 2025.
- The headline percentages apply to Amazon Linux and can be smaller for other operating systems, Regions, instance sizes, and pricing arrangements.
- The price cut does not cover every NVIDIA-powered EC2 family, including G4dn, G5, G6, G6e, G7, G7e, or the newer P6 families.
- A cheaper GPU-hour does not automatically mean a cheaper training run, inference request, or complete AI system because storage, networking, software, idle time, and managed-service fees remain separate costs.

...

| EC2 family | NVIDIA GPU | Typical workload fit | Maximum AWS-announced reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P4d | A100 | Machine-learning training, inference, and HPC | Up to 33% |
| P4de | Higher-memory A100 configuration | Large-model training, inference, and HPC workloads needing more GPU memory | Up to 33% |
| P5 | H100 | Large-scale AI training and inference | Up to 45% |
| P5en | H200 | Memory-intensive AI and HPC workloads | Up to 26% |

The GPU model alone does not identify the least expensive option. A lower-priced A100 instance may take longer to complete a training run than an H100 or H200 instance, while a higher-memory configuration may avoid model sharding or offloading. Compare dollars per completed job, not only dollars per hour.

...

AWS announced reductions of up to 45% for P5, up to 26% for P5en, and up to 33% for P4d and P4de. The qualifying phrase “up to” is important: AWS did not state that every instance size, Region, operating system, or tenancy received the maximum reduction.

AWS’s announcement does not provide a complete historical and current hourly-price table. Therefore, an exact hourly saving cannot be stated responsibly without specifying the instance size, Region, operating system, tenancy, and purchase model and then comparing the applicable AWS price records. Use the EC2 On-Demand pricing page and AWS’s Price List files or Price List API guidance for a configuration-specific calculation.

...

## When did the EC2 NVIDIA price cut take effect?

The reduced On-Demand pricing began on June 1, 2025. AWS published the announcement on June 5, 2025, so the announcement date was four days after the On-Demand effective date. AWS said the corresponding Savings Plan pricing applied to purchases made after June 4, 2025. The dates and scope are documented in AWS’s pricing announcement.

| Date | What happened | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| June 1, 2025 | Reduced On-Demand pricing began for the affected families. | Eligible usage from this date used the reduced On-Demand pricing, subject to the relevant configuration. |
| June 4, 2025 | Updated pricing applied to new Savings Plan purchases. | Commitment calculations made after this date should use the new applicable rates. |
| June 5, 2025 | AWS published the announcement. | This is the publication date, not the On-Demand effective date. |
| June 17, 2025 | AWS announced one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for P5 and P5en. | This was a later commitment-option update, separate from the original four-family price reduction. |

...

AWS applied the reduced pricing to Savings Plan purchases made after June 4, 2025, and on June 17, 2025, AWS announced one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for P5 and P5en in all Regions where those families were available. AWS advertised savings of up to 40% versus On-Demand for that one-year option, but the maximum is not an automatic 40% discount for every customer or configuration.

...

The June 2025 announcement was not a blanket reduction across AWS’s NVIDIA catalog. AWS’s accelerated-computing catalog includes G4dn, G5, G5g, G6, G6e, G6f, Gr6, G7, G7e, P4d, P4de, P5, P5en, and newer P6 families, along with non-NVIDIA accelerated instances. The announcement specifically covered only P4d, P4de, P5, and P5en.

G6f and Gr6f fractional-GPU configurations can be relevant when a full GPU would be wasteful; AWS lists profiles as small as one-eighth of an NVIDIA L4 GPU. Those fractional instances were not included in the June 2025 four-family price reduction. Review the AWS accelerated-computing catalog rather than assuming that a different NVIDIA-backed family received the same discount.

The P6-B200 update in the same AWS announcement should also be separated from the price cut. AWS made EC2 Instance Savings Plans available for P6-B200 instances, which had initially been offered through Capacity Blocks for ML; that was a purchasing-model change, not a stated reduction in the hourly price of P6-B200.

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP: H100 GPU Pricing 2026
results.author: Marcus Chen
highlights:
On eight-GPU H100 nodes, AWS lists $6.88 per GPU-hour and Azure’s cheapest US regions work out to $12.29, a 1.79x gap. AWS’s figure is the p5.48xlarge in US East (N. Virginia), checked on 11 November 2026. Azure’s is the ND96isr H100 v5 at $98.32 an hour for eight GPUs, as listed by azurespeed.com, an unofficial tracker whose listing carries no check date, so confirm the current figure on Microsoft’s Virtual Machine series pricing page before quoting it. The $6.98 Azure price that also carries an H100 label is a different machine: the NC40ads H100 v5, which has one GPU. Within the figures below, ratios of 3x or more appear only in Azure’s priciest regions or against a market median. Google Cloud is not priced in this comparison: it sells the H100 as A3 High and A3 Mega machine types, so price the exact SKU and region on Google’s own pricing page.

...

| Cloud | Instance | Node per hour | Per GPU-hour | Ratio to AWS | Month (730 h) | Year (8,760 h) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | p5.48xlarge, 8 x H100 SXM 80 GB, US East (N. Virginia) | $55.04 | $6.88 | 1.00x | $40,179.20 | $482,150.40 |
| Azure | ND96isr H100 v5, cheapest US regions | $98.32 | $12.29 | 1.79x | $71,773.60 | $861,283.20 |

...

Google’s GPU documentation lists A3 Mega (nvidia-h100-mega-80gb) and A3 High (nvidia-h100-80gb) as its H100 SXM machine families, and a3-highgpu-8g has 8 H100 GPUs with 640 GB of GPU memory. As of 12 November 2026, the same page says Google’s A4 (B200) machine types can be provisioned with reserved capacity, Spot VMs, Flex-start VMs or a MIG resize request.

Network bandwidth differs by SKU. As of 12 November 2026, Google’s GPU network bandwidth page lists A3 Mega (H100 80GB) at 1,800 Gbps with GPUDirect-TCPXO and A3 High at 1,000 Gbps with GPUDirect-TCPX. Ask each vendor what network bandwidth comes with the price you are quoted.

On AWS, aicomputeradar.dev’s 12 November 2026 listings per GPU-hour are L40S $1.86, A100 $2.74, H100 $6.88, H200 $7.91 and B200 $14.24. H200 is 15% above H100 and B200 is 2.07x. The site also reports that AWS was not the cheapest source on any class it tracks that day. For Blackwell capacity, AWS’s EC2 Capacity Blocks documentation lists P6-B200 instances as supported, and newer P6-B300 and P6e-GB200 instances are also listed.

...

Before signing, get these in writing: the exact SKU (SXM or NVL, A3 High or A3 Mega), the region, the quota and capacity the vendor will reserve for you, the networking bundle included in the price, and the date the price was quoted. Prices here are list prices from the sources named; the AWS listings are dated 11 to 13 November 2026. For how the three clouds compare on market share and growth rather than price, see our cloud market share report.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing in 2026: Why AI Compute Costs Keep Rising
highlights:
1. GPU cloud pricing reversed course: On July 1, 2026, AWS raised reserved GPU rates by roughly 20%, its second increase this year. Two decades of steadily falling cloud prices have gone into reverse, and budgets built on the old playbook no longer hold.
2. The GPU shortage is now a memory shortage: GPU die output has stabilized, but high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the new bottleneck. HBM capacity sits with a handful of suppliers and takes years to expand, so constrained supply will define 2026 and beyond.
3. Centralized costs hide beyond the rate card: Idle reservations, egress fees, and single-point pricing power inflate AI compute costs well past the hourly figure. When one vendor raises rates, every customer absorbs the shock at once.
4. A decentralized GPU cloud absorbs the shock: Aethir aggregates enterprise GPU capacity from independent operators across 94 countries into one on-demand network.
5. Treat AI infrastructure as a portfolio: Separate training from inference, run agents on Aethir Claw, and consolidate open-source model access through Aethir Mesh.

...

On July 1, 2026, Amazon Web Services raised rates for EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reservation service for AI accelerators, by roughly 20%, only six months after a 15% rise in January. Teams that reserve cloud GPU capacity have watched GPU cloud pricing climb by more than a third since the year began, and AI compute costs are rising across every roadmap that depends on reserved capacity.

Blackwell B300 instances moved to $14.04 per accelerator hour, while H100-based P5 capacity climbed to $5.191 dollars per hour in US regions. These are the most sought-after accelerators in the cloud GPU market.
